tagline.text: A church half-buried in volcanic mud, where prayers still continue

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800–2,000 per person (day trip from Manila)

children.text: A Spanish-era church about half-buried, by height, in lahar (volcanic mudflow) that swept in after the eruption of Mount Pinatubo. What were once windows now serve as doorways, and Mass is still held in front of a golden altar dug free of the mud and restored.

San Guillermo Church is an old Augustinian church in Bacolor, Pampanga, commonly called Bacolor Church or the "Half-Buried Church." Bacolor is one of the oldest towns in the Philippines, founded in the

, and the church was first built around that time on land donated by landowner Guillermo Manabat — the source of the church's name, San Guillermo (Saint William). The current stone building was rebuilt around
after the earlier church collapsed in an
earthquake, marked by a round octagonal bell tower and Baroque-Rococo ornamentation.
Bacolor was once at the center of Philippine history. When British forces occupied Manila from
to

, acting Governor-General Simon de Anda moved the Spanish colonial government here, making it a de facto temporary capital of the Philippines, and it remained the capital of Pampanga for a long stretch until the seat moved to San Fernando in
. It's also one of only three towns in the Philippines ever granted the title of Villa by the Spanish crown.
What changed its fate was the great eruption of Mount Pinatubo in
. For several years afterward, every wet season brought muddy lahar — a mix of volcanic ash and sand — pouring down the rivers onto the plain, and a major lahar flow in particular in
September 1995
buried the town, submerging about half of the church, which stands roughly
tall. Tens of thousands of residents left the town, but the faithful who stayed dug out the altar and statues and kept worshipping, using what were originally second-floor windows as the entrance.

The interior, where the ceiling feels almost within reach, the arches barely rising above ground, and the half-buried bell tower together show both the scale of the disaster and people's resilience. A visit takes about
1–2 hours

, making it easy to set aside half a day on a San Fernando or Clark trip and pair it with nearby Cabetican Shrine and Betis Church in Guagua. It leaves a particularly strong impression on travelers interested in history, architecture, and life after disaster.

blocks.title: The church you enter through a window

children.text: The original main entrance lies buried beneath the lahar, so you now enter through the arch that was once a second-floor window. The Latin inscription above the facade, Rex Regum et Dominus Dominantium ("King of Kings and Lord of Lords"), now sits at near eye level, driving home just how deep the burial goes.
The gilded altarpiece (retablo) and statues, dug out of the mud by parishioners, have been restored to their places. The altar gleaming beneath the low ceiling is the church's most moving sight.

blocks.title: Viewing the burial cross-section beside the church

children.text: Walk around the open lot beside the church and behind it to compare how far below the original ground level lies. Walk along the half-buried windows and walls to gauge just how high the lahar piled up.

A small museum set up in the old convent space displays the church's history, photos of the Pinatubo eruption and lahar damage, and old liturgical tools and statues. Hours can be irregular, so check with the church office.

blocks.title: Photographing the octagonal bell tower and facade

children.text: The round octagonal bell tower standing beside the Baroque facade looks its best in the afternoon light. Shooting from a low angle in the garden near the entrance brings out how deep the burial is.

blocks.title: Cabetican Shrine of Our Lady of Lourdes

children.text: Another buried shrine, about
15 minutes
on foot from the church. Its entrance, originally 6–7m tall, now shows barely 1m above ground, driving home the power of the lahar all over again.

A monument honoring Bacolor's history as the temporary capital of the Philippines during the British occupation. Passing through the town center, stop by briefly and consider why Bacolor earned the title of Villa.

If you're starting from Manila, leaving early in the morning to see Bacolor in the morning, then continuing to San Fernando's heritage district or Clark in the afternoon, makes for a full day.
From Cubao or Pasay in Manila, take a bus bound for San Fernando, or one bound for Olongapo/Bataan, and get off in San Fernando. It takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours 30 minutes

7–8km
and get off at Cabambangan crossing. It takes
15–25 minutes

To combine the church, Cabetican Shrine, and Betis Church, an hourly tricycle charter is convenient. A full loop costs about
— settle the route and fare before you set off.
The Pampanga plain has a dry season,
November–April
, with little rain and clear skies, good for facade photos.
December–February
is relatively cool, comfortable to explore even at midday, while
March–May
sees midday temperatures climb to
, making the church surroundings, with little shade, very hot. Visit early in the morning or late in the afternoon.
In the
June–October

rainy season, showers and typhoons are frequent, and the river basins on the Pinatubo side still sometimes get flood warnings in heavy rain. The church gets crowded with Masses and processions on the feast day of its patron saint, St. William (whom locals call Apung Gemon), on
February 10
, at the La Naval festival every
third Sunday of November
, and during Holy Week and the Christmas season, so if you want to look around quietly, a weekday morning is best.

Bacolor has almost no lodging for travelers, so most visitors come for the day. It's common to stay at a business hotel around SM City Pampanga or Robinsons Starmills in San Fernando, about
15–20 minutes
away by car (about
per night), or at a hotel or resort in Clark/Angeles, about
40 minutes
away. If you're flying through Clark Airport, it fits well as a half-day trip on your arrival or departure day.

Eat in neighboring Guagua or San Fernando. Guagua is known for its simple, soft halo-halo, topped with little more than finely shaved ice, banana, leche flan, and macapuno, and for traditional pastries, while San Fernando has old restaurants like Everybody's Cafe, open since

, serving classic Kapampangan dishes. Be sure to also try buro, a fermented-rice Pampanga dish, sweet tocino and longganisa, and sisig from its birthplace, Angeles. Around the church itself, there are only small shops selling simple snacks and drinks.
The church is still an active parish. Avoid sleeveless tops or short shorts, and refrain from taking photos during Mass.
The museum is sometimes closed. Ask the church office or caretaker politely — they may open it for you.
To capture just how deep the burial is, try photographing the half-buried windows and arches together from the open lot beside the church.
Cabetican Shrine is about
15 minutes
on foot, but there's little shade along the way. Take a tricycle at midday.
Betis Church in Guagua, known as the "Sistine Chapel of the Philippines" for its lavish ceiling paintings, is nearby — be sure to visit it too.
Return transport can be scarce, so if you took a Grab, agree with the driver in advance on waiting and a round trip.
Small shops and tricycles take cash only. Keep some small change ready for donations too.
Jeepneys from San Fernando to Guagua along the Old National Highway pass through Bacolor town, so you can get off close to the church. It helps to tell the driver "Bacolor Church" when you board.
Some parts of the church interior have low ceilings and dim lighting. Watch your head and step.
At midday in
March–May
, the church surroundings, with little shade, get very hot. Bring a hat and water.
During heavy rain in the wet season, rivers in the Pinatubo basin can rise and flood roads. Postpone your visit if a typhoon or heavy rain is forecast.
Viewing may be limited during Mass, weddings, or funerals. Don't disturb the service — wait it out.
Museum hours and donation amounts can change. Check the parish's latest notices before you visit.
Bacolor sits low even after the lahar built up around it and floods often. In the
August 2026

southwest monsoon downpour, the Cabetican shrine was flooded up to chest height and schools around Kabambangan, where the church stands, were closed for several days. In the rainy season, check the notices on the Bacolor municipal
official website
